title: wind, breath and fire
hook: the third name nobody explained, and what speaking in tongues is
tomorrow: a library that tells one story

segments.voice: Yesterday: testimony, a witness statement. Today, the third name in the blessing from day two.

Of the three names, Father and Son come with pictures. The Holy Spirit can feel like the one nobody explained. Maybe you saw people speaking in tongues at a friend's church and wondered what was happening. Maybe you wondered why it never happened to you. The words underneath are plainer than you'd think: breath, and wind.

In Hebrew the word is ruach; in Greek, pneuma. Both mean breath, wind and spirit, all at once. On the Bible's first page, the spirit of God, or the wind of God, moves over the waters. In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus breathes on his friends and says: receive the Holy Spirit. Jesus calls the Spirit the Paraclete: the one called alongside you. A helper, an advocate, someone in your corner. Then fire. Fifty days after Passover, at the festival of Pentecost, his friends hear a sound like a rushing wind, something like flames rests on each of them, and they speak in languages the visiting crowd can understand. Speaking in tongues today is understood in different ways. Pentecostal and charismatic churches treasure it as a living gift, often as a way of praying. Some churches believe that gift belonged mainly to the first generation; many others are open to it but rarely practice it. And Paul, writing to a church that prized it, asks: "do all speak with tongues?" He expects the answer no. His list of what the Spirit grows is quieter: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness.

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, just notice the air: in, and out. On the second, remember that in the old languages, breath and spirit are one word. On the third, breathe slowly, and let it be enough.
The Holy Spirit. Ruach, pneuma: breath, wind, spirit, the helper called alongside. Sixth word.
Your line: closer than your own breath. In the old languages, it's the same word. See you on day seven.

howItsDone: Christians pray to and through the Holy Spirit and celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter; in Pentecostal and charismatic churches, speaking in tongues, healing prayer and prophecy are part of worship, while many other churches pray more quietly for the Spirit's gifts and fruit.

fork.setup: Jesus's friends are together at Pentecost. a sound like a rushing wind fills the house. what happens next?
options: something like flames rests on each of them, and they speak in languages the crowd understands.
fork.reveal: wind, then fire, then words every visitor could understand. it's often called the birthday of the church.

original.note: Hebrew: breath, wind, spirit. Greek holds the same three in one word: pneuma.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ghost, or a feeling at a loud worship night.
what it means: God's own breath and presence, the helper called alongside.
what a scholar hears: ruach (Hebrew) and pneuma (Greek) both mean breath, wind and spirit; parakletos, an advocate (John 14–16); glossolalia, 'tongue-speech', in Acts 2 and 1 Corinthians 12–14.

story.title: nine in the morning
story.text: A roar like a rushing wind sends a crowd running through the streets of Jerusalem. They find a small group of Galileans pouring out of a house, talking, and every visitor hears them in their own language, from Egypt to Rome. Some are amazed. Others laugh: they've had too much new wine. Then Peter stands up and says, more or less: it's nine in the morning. And he gives the first sermon of the church.

wrong.myth: the Holy Ghost is something spooky.
wrong.truth: ghost is older English for spirit. underneath it is the word for breath.

notes: New lesson (2026-10-06), written from the audience research: the Holy Spirit and speaking in tongues (GotQuestions top 20, #12; the Quora worry 'I can't speak in tongues, does that mean I haven't received the Spirit?'; proposed day 6).

Sensitive: classical Pentecostal churches (e.g. the Assemblies of God) teach tongues as the initial evidence of Spirit baptism, a separate experience from conversion; cessationist churches hold the gift ended with the apostles. The script says 'Pentecostal and charismatic churches treasure it… some churches believe it belonged mainly to the first generation; many others are open to it but rarely practice it', and uses Paul's question without ruling. Please check that Pentecostal readers recognize themselves.
1 Corinthians 12:30 is a rhetorical question expecting 'no' in the Greek (μὴ). Confirm.
Galatians 5:22 fruit list paraphrased in modern words (KJV: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith).
Pentecost (Shavuot) is fifty days after Passover; the Christian feast is fifty days after Easter (howItsDone). Confirm both are stated correctly.
Story card: Acts 2:15, 'it is but the third hour of the day', rendered as nine in the morning.
